OraLab User Guide

OraLab 1.0.11 — a workbench for tuning Oracle SQL. Run one statement step by step as you change it, keep the statistics, waits and execution plan of every step, put two runs side by side, and save them as Excel, PDF or HTML.

1. What OraLab is

Tuning steps as tabsEvery change to the SQL gets its own tab (sql_01, sql_02 …). Script, memo, note and result are saved automatically — open it days later and it is all still there.
Measured on the serverOraLab wraps your SQL in a trace script and sends it to the server. Session statistic deltas (V$MYSTAT), wait events, V$SQL and the actual execution plan (DBMS_XPLAN) come back in one run and are shown as tables.
Two runs, side by sideCompare two tabs, or two SQL_IDs (cursor cache or AWR), by Metrics · Plan · Waits · Statistics, and save the comparison as an Excel, PDF or HTML report.
  • One Windows (x64) program, OraLab.exe. Nothing to install; no Oracle client and no SQL*Plus needed.
  • The SQL runs to the end, fetching every row — the numbers are not those of a first screenful. The rows themselves are not shown: OraLab looks at what the SQL cost and which plan it used, not at its result.
  • Every run ends with a ROLLBACK, so that a tuning experiment leaves no data behind (the implicit commit of DDL cannot be undone).

2. Getting started

  1. Unzip OraLab.zip and start OraLab.exe. If the Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime is missing, a window tells you where to get it (Windows 11 ships with it).
  2. In Connections, fill in Host · Port · Service · User · Password. Name is what the list shows (optional). For a saved connection the Password box is empty and shows masking dots (••••••••) — leave it empty to use the saved password, or type a new one to replace it; the saved password is never shown again. To remove the saved password, press the ✕ at the right of the box, then Save (or Connect). To use a tnsnames alias or a full descriptor, put it in Data source.
  3. Tick the packs this server is licensed for — Diagnostics Pack licensed (AWR · ASH) and Tuning Pack licensed (SQL Monitor reports). OraLab does not read the features of a pack that is not ticked. The Tuning Pack requires the Diagnostics Pack, so its box can be ticked only when the first one is.
  4. Press Connect (or Enter, or double-click a connection). When you land in CDB$ROOT, Select Container asks which PDB to work in.
  • + New · Copy · Delete manage several connections. Save stores without connecting.
  • Test (bottom left): connects with the values entered, shows the server version and disconnects — nothing is saved and the window stays open.
  • Connections that need a wallet (mTLS on Autonomous Database and the like): unzip the wallet into a folder, paste the entry from tnsnames.ora into Data source as a whole, and name that folder with my_wallet_directory in the security part. If you paste the leading name = too, OraLab removes it. The top row and the list show the address inside the descriptor as host:port/service. 
    (description=
  (retry_count=20)(retry_delay=3)
  (address=(protocol=tcps)(port=1522)(host=adb.ap-seoul-1.oraclecloud.com))
  (connect_data=(service_name=xxxxxxxx_mydb_tp.adb.oraclecloud.com))
  (security=(ssl_server_dn_match=yes)(my_wallet_directory=D:\Oracle\wallet_mydb)))
  • The window opens on every start with the last connection selected — Enter is enough.
  • Switching servers: Connection in the top row of the main window opens this window again. Connect to another connection and the window stays; tasks and tabs are redrawn for the new server (each tab still records the server it ran on). It cannot be pressed while a run or tuning is in progress. An open SQLID History window keeps reading the server it was opened on.
  • Connection dot: the dot before the address is blue when connected and red when disconnected. Click blue to disconnect (a running run is cancelled, and nothing goes to the server until you connect again); click red to connect to the same server again.
  • Only one OraLab runs per folder; starting it again brings the running window forward. To watch two servers at once, copy the exe into a second folder.

3. The screen

WhereWhat
Top rowThe connection dot (blue connected · red disconnected) · the server you are connected to (user@address — the OraLab version, connection name and server version are in the window title, with Exadata before the version on Exadata) · the Task list (with + New task… and More… at the bottom) · Connection (switch servers, chapter 2) · SQLID Compare · SQLID → Tab · SQLID History (chapter 9) · Export Base Script · Close (exits OraLab) · theme (12) · GitHub (opens the public repository in the browser)
Tab rowThe tabs of this task. Next to the name: the status (✓ ok · ✗ error) and the elapsed time; a tab not run yet says editing. + adds a tab with a copy of the current script
Run rowRun (F8) / Cancel while running · Beautify · the memo (one line: what changed in this step) · on the right the status · elapsed · SQL_ID · child · plan hash · start time
Sub-tabsScript · Summary · Statistics · Waits · V$SQL · DBMS_XPLAN · Bind Variables · ASH · SQL Monitor · QB Registry · Optimizer Env · Objects · Plan Fix · Tuning Advisor · Raw Output · Note. Parts missing from this output, and tools that cannot be used here, are dimmed

4. Running SQL

4.1 Running a single SQL statement

Put one SELECT SQL in the Script sub-tab and press Run (F8) (or Ctrl+Enter). OraLab wraps it in the base script (chapter 11) and runs it. When it finishes you are taken to Summary. The first tab of a new task starts with a sample SQL (SELECT * FROM USER_TABLES) and comment lines that show the <Commands> Â· <Variables> blocks.

  • A trailing ; is optional. Comments in front of the SQL may stay.
  • While it runs, Cancel and the elapsed time replace Run, and the output streams into the Raw Output sub-tab.
  • Closing the window while a run or Tuning Advisor is in progress cancels it first and waits up to 5 seconds for it to stop. Text still being typed in Script, the memo or Note is saved before the window closes.
  • A single DML, DDL or WITH FUNCTION statement is not run — OraLab explains why. To run the SQL to the end it is placed in a PL/SQL cursor, and only SELECT · WITH fit there. Run such statements as a script (4.4).
  • Beautify changes only spaces and line breaks, never a character of the SQL. It formats the selection, or — in a tab that holds only a query — the SQL part even with nothing selected (<Variables> and <Commands> blocks are left alone).
  • Parallelism, SQL monitoring and hints are whatever you wrote. OraLab does not edit your SQL.

4.2 Running with bind variables — <Variables>

Replacing binds with literals can give a plan different from production. Put a <Variables> block at the very top of the tab and declare PL/SQL variables in it; wherever the SQL uses one of those names, it is passed as a bind variable (no colon in the SQL — just the variable name).

<Variables>
  b_status       VARCHAR2(10)   := 'ACTIVE';
  b_from         DATE           := TO_DATE('2026-01-01', 'YYYY-MM-DD');
</Variables>

SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, o.order_date, o.total_amount
  FROM dbcopy.customers c, dbcopy.orders_part o
 WHERE c.status = b_status
   AND c.created_at >= b_from
   AND o.customer_id (+) = c.customer_id
  • On the server the statement shows :B1, :B2 (the SQL text and Peeked Binds in DBMS_XPLAN).
  • The declarations are plain PL/SQL. A wrong declaration or an undeclared name gives you Oracle's own error.
  • If a variable has the same name as a column of the table, Oracle reads it as the column — no error, a different predicate (WHERE status = status). Use a prefix such as b_.
  • To bring in the bind values a statement really ran with, use SQLID → Tab (chapter 8).

4.3 Session commands — <Commands>

To run the SQL under different session parameters, write the statements in a <Commands> block. Where the block sits decides when it runs: a block before the SQL runs before the test SQL, a block after the SQL runs once the measuring is over — both in the same session. Each run opens a new connection, so nothing carries over to the next run.

<Commands>
  ALTER SESSION SET "_serial_direct_read" = true;
  ALTER SESSION SET optimizer_mode = FIRST_ROWS_1;
</Commands>

SELECT /*+ MONITOR */ a.owner, COUNT(*) cnt
  FROM all_objects a
 GROUP BY a.owner
  • There can be one <Commands> block before the SQL and one after it. Settings meant to affect the measurement must go before the SQL — a block after it runs once the measuring is over and does not show in the result.
  • <Variables> works the same before or after the SQL. No block can sit in the middle of the SQL.
  • End each SQL statement with ;.
  • The blocks work only in a tab that holds one SELECT SQL. In a tab that holds the whole base script, OraLab does not run and says why — put the settings into the script itself there.
  • A PL/SQL block (BEGIN … END;) is fine too. When the block comes last it needs no / line. When more statements follow a block, put a / line between them, as in SQL*Plus.
  • If any command fails, the run stops there and shows Oracle's error — so that nothing is measured under settings that did not take effect. @file, START, !command and HOST lines and CONNECT are not run by OraLab, so they stop the run with an error (ORA-20001); put the file's statements in the block instead.
  • When the block after the SQL does not run: if you cancel the run, if a command in the block before the SQL fails, or if the connection drops, the run stops and the <Commands> block after the SQL is not run. ALTER SESSION settings need no undoing — each run uses a new connection. If a PL/SQL block creates an object on the server and the block after the SQL drops it, clean up what is left yourself after such a stop.
  • What the block takes: only ALTER SESSION and PL/SQL blocks. Other statements such as CREATE, DROP, ALTER TABLE, ALTER INDEX and DML stop the run with an error (ORA-20001) before measuring. If you really need one, put it in a PL/SQL block with EXECUTE IMMEDIATE; any change it leaves on the server is yours to clean up.
  • The settings that took effect show in the Optimizer Env sub-tab after the run (it lists the non-default values).
  • The commands stay with the result — above the Test SQL in Summary, in the tab's Excel, PDF and HTML, and in the SQL tab of Compare, under -- Commands (before) and -- Commands after the SQL (after). The settings a result came from are read together with its SQL.

Sample 1 — variables, commands before, commands after. The settings of the block in front apply to the measurement; the block at the end runs after it.

<Variables>
  v1             VARCHAR2(10)   := 'TABLE';
</Variables>

<Commands>
  ALTER SESSION SET "_serial_direct_read" = true;
  ALTER SESSION SET optimizer_mode = FIRST_ROWS_1;
</Commands>

SELECT /*+ MONITOR */ a.owner, COUNT(*) cnt
  FROM all_objects a
 WHERE a.object_type = v1
 GROUP BY a.owner
 ORDER BY 2 DESC

<Commands>
  ALTER SESSION SET "_rowsource_execution_statistics" = FALSE;
</Commands>

Sample 2 — a PL/SQL block. A setting that may fail in some environments can be wrapped in a block that catches the exception, so the run does not stop. The block comes last, so it needs no / line.

<Commands>
  ALTER SESSION SET "_serial_direct_read" = true;
  ALTER SESSION SET optimizer_mode = FIRST_ROWS_1;

  BEGIN
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'alter session set CELL_OFFLOAD_PROCESSING = TRUE';
  EXCEPTION
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
      DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE($$PLSQL_UNIT || ' : ' || DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_STACK);
  END;
</Commands>

Sample 3 — statements after a block. A block ends at a line holding only /. To write more statements after a block, put a / line between them.

<Commands>
  BEGIN
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'alter session set CELL_OFFLOAD_PROCESSING = TRUE';
  END;
  /
  ALTER SESSION SET optimizer_mode = FIRST_ROWS_1;
</Commands>
Without the / line, the ALTER SESSION … after END; is read as part of the block: Oracle reports the compile error PLS-00103 and the run stops. With several blocks, put a / line after each; only the last one may go without.

4.4 Running the whole base script

OraLab runs one SELECT SQL inside the cursor of the base script (OraLab.sql) and analyses it. Put one SELECT SQL in a tab. More than one SELECT SQL, PL/SQL blocks, DML and SQL*Plus commands are not run; the notice line says why.

  • A tab holding the whole base script (for example OraLab.sql saved with Export Base Script) runs the whole script only when the text between [TEST SQL QUERY START] and [TEST SQL QUERY END] (the cursor) is one SELECT SQL. The result is split into sub-tabs.
  • Session: one run is one session, and each run opens a new connection, so an ALTER SESSION does not carry over. Put session settings for the measurement in a <Commands> block (4.3).

5. Reading the result

5.1 Summary sub-tab and table sorting

Summary shows the status, start time, elapsed time, SQL_ID, child number and plan hash value; the Test SQL that was run (the commands of <Commands>, the declarations and the SQL — Beautify here changes the view only); and the closing lines of the script (Trace Run Time · DB · SID). Test SQL is the text that produced this result, not whatever is in the editor now.

Every table sorts when you click a header (first click: numeric columns largest first, text columns alphabetical → second click: reversed → third click: original order). Sorting is on screen only; Excel, PDF and HTML keep the original order.

5.2 Statistics · Waits · V$SQL sub-tabs

Sub-tabContent
StatisticsThe difference in session statistics across the test SQL (V$MYSTAT, plus GV$PX_SESSTAT of the PX slaves when parallel). The upper table is a summary — Buffer Hit Ratio · Recursive Calls · PGA · temp reads and writes · logical and physical reads. On Exadata, Smart Scan · Storage Index · HCC · Flash Cache items and an Assessment column are added ([OPTIMAL] green · [FAIR] amber · warnings red). The last summary line, 34.Sequence Load Elapsed Time(sec), is the time spent refilling sequence caches (V$SESS_TIME_MODEL — OraLab reads it before and after the run). It appears only from 0.001 s — when it does, a sequence with a small cache or NOCACHE was called many times. It covers the whole run, so sequences used in <Commands> count too. A parallel SELECT is covered as well — the QC calls NEXTVAL (SEQUENCE sits above PX COORDINATOR in the plan). ALL V$MYSTAT delta below lists every non-zero statistic, for tabs that hold only SQL
WaitsThe difference in this session's wait events (V$SESSION_EVENT) — Event · Class · Waits · Time(ms) · Avg(ms)
V$SQLThe V$SQL figures of this cursor, per execution — Elapsed · CPU · Buffer Gets · Disk Reads · Rows and more. When it ran in parallel, PX Execs / exec (executions by PX servers per execution — PX_SERVERS_EXECUTIONS ÷ executions, not the number of PX servers) is added and Elapsed Time Sec is the sum of the QC and PX server times; the time it actually took is ELAPSED below
ASHThe share of ASH samples per plan line — where the time went (on a connection with Diagnostics Pack ticked). Samples are one second apart, so a run shorter than a second shows nothing
SQL MonitorThe SQL Monitor report when this run was monitored (parallel, longer than 5 seconds, or a MONITOR hint — on a connection with Tuning Pack ticked)
QB RegistryQuery Block Registry (19c and later) — the block names after query transformation
Optimizer EnvThe optimizer environment of this cursor (V$SQL_OPTIMIZER_ENV) — non-default values only
Raw OutputThe complete text the server printed. Lines that could not be read into a table are still here

5.3 DBMS_XPLAN sub-tab

  • These are the actual run statistics of DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR — E-Rows (estimated) and A-Rows (actual) on the same line.
  • Line colours: full scans light red, index range scans blue, unique scans and nested loops green, SORT amber, a serial step inside a parallel plan and Cartesian joins dark red and bold.
  • The sections below (Query Block Name · Outline Data · Peeked Binds · Predicate Information · Column Projection · Note · Hint Report) are collapsed; click a title to open it. Predicate Information starts open.
  • Ctrl+A here selects the plan text only — handy for pasting elsewhere.

5.4 Bind Variables sub-tab

Collects every set of bind values the server keeps for this tab's SQL_ID — for a tab made with SQLID → Tab, the original SQL_ID. Use it to pick the values to run with.

  • The list picks a set — each monitored run in SQL Monitor (slowest first, Tuning Pack), each child in the cursor cache capture, each AWR snapshot (Diagnostics Pack). Nothing is read from a pack that is not ticked.
  • The table shows the type and value of each bind. For a tab made with SQLID → Tab, the value in this tab's <Variables> is shown beside it, in orange when it differs.
  • Declare · Inline switch the text below. Declare declares the values as variables so the binds stay binds; Inline puts each value in as a literal (a literal can get a different plan than a bind).
  • New tab opens the text below in a new tab; this tab is not changed. Run it there with F8, then compare with Compare with….
  • Read from the server when first opened; Reload reads again. Not saved — read again after a restart.

5.5 Note sub-tab

The Note sub-tab holds the long explanation of a step (what was tuned and why). It saves itself; a dot next to the sub-tab name says there is text. The note goes into the tab's Excel, PDF and HTML and appears above the SQL in Compare. The memo in the Run row is a one-line tag — shown in the tab's tooltip and under the report title.

5.6 Objects sub-tab

OraLab finds the tables in the executed plan (V$SQL_PLAN) and reads their statistics from the dictionary (ALL_* views). Nothing is guessed from the SQL text, so you see the real tables behind views and synonyms.

TableColumns
TablesOwner · Table · Rows · Blocks · Avg row len · Last analyzed · Stale · Partitions · Partition key · Subpartition key · Subpartitions · Stale parts · No-stats parts · Degree · Compression · In-Memory · Cell flash cache
IndexesEvery index of those tables — a ● under Used marks the ones this plan used. Type · Unique · Columns · Compression · Distinct keys · Clustering factor · BLevel · Leaf blocks · Rows · Status · Visibility · Last analyzed
Predicate columnsOnly the columns in the plan's access and filter predicates — Type · Null · NDV · Nulls · Density · Histogram · Buckets · Low · High · Last analyzed · Indexes (which indexes hold the column, and at which position) · Expression (of a virtual column)
  • Read once when you first open the sub-tab, then kept with the tab. After gathering statistics again, press Reload. Running the tab again clears it.
  • For a partitioned table, Compression · In-Memory · Cell flash cache are collected from its partitions — mixed values are listed with their counts.
  • In-Memory is the attribute declared on the table, not whether the segment is populated right now.
  • Tables this account cannot see are listed under Not shown.
  • Nothing is read when the tab was run on a server other than the one you are connected to now.

5.7 Plan Fix sub-tab

A script text for when you want to pin the plan of this tab to a statement in production. OraLab does not run it. Read it, take it where it belongs, and run it yourself (Ctrl+A, then copy).

  • 1. SQL Patch (DBMS_SQLDIAG.CREATE_SQL_PATCH, 12.2 and later) — attaches the Outline Data hints of this plan to the SQL_ID. The Check and Undo statements are there as comments.
  • 2. SQL Plan Baseline (DBMS_SPM.LOAD_PLANS_FROM_CURSOR_CACHE, Enterprise Edition) — loads this plan from the cursor cache as a baseline.
  • 3. SQL Profile (DBMS_SQLTUNE.IMPORT_SQL_PROFILE, force_match => TRUE, Tuning Pack) — attaches the same Outline hints as a SQL profile. Unlike the SQL patch and the baseline, it also applies to statements that differ only in literals. Shown only on a connection with Tuning Pack ticked. IMPORT_SQL_PROFILE is not in the Oracle documentation; Oracle Support's coe_xfr_sql_profile.sql uses it.
  • To pin a plan you got with hints to the original statement without them, change the lines marked << (the SQL_ID) to those of the original. Both statements must have the same query blocks and aliases, or the hints will not be picked up.
  • Both take effect at the next hard parse of the statement.

5.8 Tuning Advisor sub-tab

Runs the SQL Tuning Advisor (DBMS_SQLTUNE) on the cursor this tab ran (SQL_ID and plan hash value) and shows its report — SQL profile, index, statistics and rewrite recommendations. OraLab does not apply the recommendations. Take the statements from the report and run them yourself.

  • The box at the top holds the PL/SQL to run, with the SQL_ID, plan hash value, time limit and task name written in. You can edit it, and OraLab runs your text as it is — change scope to LIMITED, for example. The report shown below is whatever the block puts into :report. If the block fails, Oracle's error is shown as it is.
  • It runs only when you press Run Tuning Advisor. For a different time limit, change time_limit in the text (60 seconds at first). Cancel stops it; F8 still works while it runs.
  • Reset script puts back the text OraLab made (with a new task name).
  • The block drops its task. If it never gets that far (an error, or Cancel), OraLab drops the ORALAB_ task named in the text once more.
  • Your text and the report are saved with the tab. Running the tab again, or Clear, removes them, and the text is made again for the new SQL_ID.
  • If the cursor has left the shared pool, run the tab again (F8) first.
  • It is available only when Tuning Pack licensed is ticked for the connection, the account has the ADVISOR privilege and execute on DBMS_SQLTUNE, and the server's control_management_pack_access allows the Tuning Pack. Otherwise it is dimmed; open it to see why.

6. Managing steps as tabs — tabs and tasks

ToDo
Start the next step+ in the tab row — a new tab with a copy of the current script. Change the hint or the SQL and Run again
RenameHold the tab down for 0.6 seconds, or Rename in the menu. Enter saves, Esc cancels
ReorderDrag the tab. Sort By Name in the menu sorts by name (numbers as numbers — sql_2 before sql_10)
DuplicateDuplicate in the menu — a tab with the same script, memo and note right next to it (the result is not copied)
Clear the result / remove the tabClear / Close in the menu (or the × on the tab)
Remove all tabs of this taskClose All in the menu — asks once. A running tab stays; when all are gone, one new tab with the sample SQL appears
Export · compareSave As Excel · Save As PDF · Save As HTML · Compare with… in the menu

Hovering over a tab shows its SQL_ID — memo as a tooltip.

A task is a group of tabs for one topic (one tuning case, one task). The list in the top row shows the recent ones; More… opens the full list — search by name, open, rename, delete. Tasks are not tied to a connection: each tab records the server it ran on.

7. Comparing runs

7.1 Comparing two tabs — Compare with…

Right-click the tab to be judged (the later step) → Compare with…, then pick the baseline. The tab you pick is A (base), the one you right-clicked is B. Tabs of other tasks can be picked too. The comparison uses the saved results — the server is not asked again.

TabContent
SQLThe SQL of A and B side by side (a tab's note sits above its SQL). Beautify / Original switches the view
MetricsV$SQL figures per execution. Where lower is better, a decrease is green and an increase red. Rows Processed is not judged
PlanBoth plans in one table, lines matched by operation and name — only the numeric columns are split into A | B. In B, ▼ green is lower and ▲ red is higher; a line on one side only is tagged A only or B only
WaitsWait events joined by name
StatisticsThe summary items (Item · A · B · B − A · %) with their assessments, then every V$MYSTAT statistic (largest |B − A| first)

Excel, PDF and HTML at the bottom save this comparison as a report.

7.2 Comparing two SQL_IDs — SQLID Compare

Statements that were never run in OraLab can be compared too. Enter two SQL_IDs in SQLID Compare in the top row — before and after a plan change in production, or a hinted statement against the original.

  • child or plan hash may stay empty: the most recently active child is used (for AWR, the latest plan). A number is tried as a child number first, then as a plan hash value.
  • Source: Cursor cache (V$SQL) · AWR · AWR when not in the cursor cache. AWR can be chosen only on a connection with Diagnostics Pack ticked.
  • On RAC, choose a Node for A and for B (ALL or an instance number; it starts at the instance you are connected to).
  • Statistics (V$MYSTAT deltas) exist only for tabs run in OraLab. Waits of a SQL_ID comparison come from ASH samples (when the pack is on).
  • Parallel runs: a side that ran in parallel has (QC + PX) after its Elapsed Time Sec and a PX Execs / exec row. Elapsed time in V$SQL and AWR is the sum of the QC and PX server times, not the time it took — for the real time of one run see the SQL Monitor tab (Duration) of SQLID History.

8. Loading a captured SQL — SQLID → Tab

Brings a statement from production into a tab together with the bind values it ran with. Enter a SQL_ID in SQLID → Tab in the top row; OraLab builds a new tab from the SQL text in the cursor cache and the captured bind values (V$SQL_BIND_CAPTURE).

  • The variable name is always the bind name with b_ in front (:B1 → b_B1, :1 → b_1) — so that it cannot collide with a column.
  • VARCHAR2 · CHAR · NUMBER · DATE · TIMESTAMP get their value. A bind that was not captured is left as NULL; -- not captured, other types as NULL; -- captured: value — check and fill in the values, then F8.
  • Where the values come from, in this order: ① SQL Monitor — the actual values of the slowest monitored run (longer than 5 seconds, parallel, or a MONITOR hint; only on a connection with Tuning Pack ticked) → ② the cursor cache capture (V$SQL_BIND_CAPTURE) → ③ AWR (DBA_HIST_SQLBIND, when the cursor is gone; only with Diagnostics Pack ticked). The comment at the top of the tab says which.
  • Captures (② and ③) are taken only at intervals and mainly for WHERE-clause binds, so they need not be the values of the run that mattered. SQL Monitor keeps its records in memory for a short time only (typically about an hour).
  • SQL Monitor TIMESTAMP values are read exactly on 19c and 12.2. On 26ai they come with a two-digit year, read by the RR rule (00–49 → 20xx, 50–99 → 19xx) with the original text kept as a comment (-- SQL Monitor: 99/01/25 …) — correct the century if needed, then F8. NUMBER values bound as binary integers come without a value and are left as NULL with a comment.
  • The tab is named after the SQL_ID. It is created, not run.
  • The SQL text arrives on one line — tidy it with Beautify.

9. AWR execution history — SQLID History

Shows in one window what AWR kept about one SQL_ID — which plans it ran with and which was fastest, when the plan changed, and what the bind values were then. SQLID History in the top row opens a separate window (a new one each time). It is not a popup, so you can move between it and the main window and copy SQL, plans and bind values across. The button works only on a connection with Diagnostics Pack ticked.

  • Top row: SQL_ID · DBID (only when both the PDB and the CDB have AWR — the PDB is the default; when PDB-level AWR is off, as by default on 19c and 12.2, the CDB's AWR is read and there is no box) · Instance (RAC only, starting at the node you are connected to) · Interval (By Day · By Hour · By Week · By Snap ID) · From (days, hours or weeks back from now; with By Snap ID a snapshot number, together with To) · Read (Enter). The default By Day · 1 is the last 24 hours. Time is counted by the server clock (SYSDATE).
  • While it reads from the server, the inputs and buttons of the top row, the sub-tabs and the save buttons at the bottom are locked, and Cancel appears in the top row. Cancel stops every read in progress.
  • Every query is limited to the chosen DBID. In a PDB, DBA_HIST_* shows both the CDB's and the PDB's AWR, so without that the same executions would be counted twice.
TabContentSource
SQLThe whole SQL text (not cut). One-line text is shown with line breaks; Beautify · OriginalDBA_HIST_SQLTEXT
PlansFor each plan hash: first and last seen, snapshots, executions, elapsed · CPU · buffers · reads · rows per execution, optimizer environment hash (orange when it differs). A plan that ran in parallel has (QC + PX) after its elapsed time — the sum of the QC and PX server times, not the time it took. Select a row for that plan (with line colours). Plan Fix — load this plan from AWR shows the DBMS_SPM.LOAD_PLANS_FROM_AWR text that loads the plan as a SQL plan baseline (12.2 and later; OraLab does not run it). Compare with reads two plans from the same DBID and range and opens them in Compare (chapter 7)DBA_HIST_SQLSTAT · DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_WORKLOAD_REPOSITORY (DISPLAY_AWR on 12.2)
BindsOne row per snapshot with the captured bind values and the plan hash that ran in that snapshot. A value different from the row below (the earlier one) is orange — match plan changes against value changes. Select a row for the Declare · Inline text; New tab opens it in the main windowDBA_HIST_SQLBIND
TrendA chart of per-execution values per snapshot (Measure: elapsed · CPU · buffers · reads · rows · executions). Line colour = plan hash, a dashed line where the plan changed. Click a point to jump to its row in the table belowDBA_HIST_SQLSTAT
ASHSamples (one per 10 s) by wait event, by plan line, by module and userDBA_HIST_ACTIVE_SESS_HISTORY
SQL MonitorPast SQL Monitor reports; select one for its text (only with Tuning Pack ticked)DBA_HIST_REPORTS · DBA_HIST_REPORTS_DETAILS
Optimizer EnvThe optimizer environment of two plans. AWR keeps only a hash of it, so the tab shows whether the hashes are equal; values are compared only while both cursors are still in the cache (differences only)DBA_HIST_SQLSTAT · V$SQL_OPTIMIZER_ENV
AWR ReportPick Begin and End snapshots and press Make report — made only then. If the instance restarted in that range, you are told before anything is runDBMS_WORKLOAD_REPOSITORY.AWR_SQL_REPORT_TEXT
  • Excel · PDF · HTML at the bottom save everything in tab order (chapter 10). The save dialog and the result line appear in this window — also when saving a Compare opened from it.
  • AWR keeps one set of bind values per snapshot, and only values that fell on a capture interval. SQL Monitor reports exist only for monitored runs (longer than 5 seconds and the like).

10. Exporting reports — Excel · PDF · HTML

WhatWhereContent
One tabSave As Excel · Save As PDF · Save As HTML in the tab menuSummary (run information · note · Test SQL) → one sheet per sub-tab (the same tables as on screen, plan line colours included) → Objects (when it has been read) → Script → Raw
A comparisonExcel · PDF · HTML at the bottom of CompareSQL → Metrics (with an Excel chart) → Plan → Waits → Statistics
SQLID HistoryExcel · PDF · HTML at the bottom of that windowSummary (what was read · SQL) → Plans (a table per plan) → Binds → Trend (with the chart in PDF · HTML) → ASH → SQL Monitor → Optimizer Env → AWR Report (only when made). Tabs not opened yet are read when saving (SQL Monitor report texts: the latest 20)
  • The suggested file name is Task_Tab_SQLID_yyyyMMdd_HHmmss, for a comparison compare_SQLID_vs_SQLID_yyyyMMdd_HHmmss, for SQLID History sqlid_history_SQLID_yyyyMMdd_HHmmss.
  • PDF pages are A4 landscape. A tab report (PDF or HTML) has a table of contents under its header; each entry links to its section.
  • HTML saves the same report as the PDF in one HTML file (styles inside, so it looks the same wherever it is opened). To print it from a browser with Ctrl+P, choose landscape and turn on background graphics to match the PDF.
  • To have Objects in the report, open the Objects sub-tab once before exporting. Tuning Advisor is included only for a tab where you ran it (exporting does not run it). Plan Fix is not exported.

11. The base script (OraLab.sql)

The measuring is done by the trace script OraLab.sql inside the exe. It takes the session statistics and waits before and after the test SQL, then prints V$SQL, DBMS_XPLAN and the rest through DBMS_OUTPUT.

  • Export Base Script in the top row writes it to a .sql file — it also runs on its own in SQL*Plus or PL/SQL Developer.
  • In the script, the test SQL goes between -- [TEST SQL QUERY START] and -- [TEST SQL QUERY END], variables between -- [VARIABLES START] and -- [VARIABLES END], session commands between -- [COMMANDS START] and -- [COMMANDS END] (the pair before the trace block for commands before, the pair after it for commands after). Do not remove these marker lines — that is where OraLab puts your SQL, variables and commands.
  • A tab that holds only SQL is always run with the script bundled in this version.

13. Files · privileges · support

13.1 Files

File (next to the exe)Content
OraLab.dbConnections (passwords encrypted) · tasks · tabs · results · window position · theme. This one file is all your work — copy it to back up or to move to another PC
OraLab.db.vN.bakA copy made just before a newer version upgrades the file. Only the newest one is kept; older copies are deleted at start
WebView2\The cache of WebView2, which draws the window. It holds no settings — you can delete it; it is made again on the next start. If the exe folder is not writable, the default location in your Windows profile is used
OraLab.logCreated only when an error occurs

13.2 Supported versions and DB privileges

  • Oracle versions: checked on 12.2, 19c and 26ai. QB Registry appears on 19c and later only.
  • Privileges: with the grants below every feature of OraLab works (checked on 12.2, 19c and 26ai with an account holding only these). The script written by Export Base Script carries the same grant statements in its header, ready to hand to a DBA.
    • Base: CREATE SESSION · SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE · SELECT ANY DICTIONARY · SELECT ANY TABLE — the performance and AWR views, and the tables and views the SQL you tune reads.
    • Tuning Advisor sub-tab: ADVISOR (ORA-13616 without it).
    • AWR Report in SQLID History: EXECUTE ON SYS.DBMS_WORKLOAD_REPOSITORY — PUBLIC cannot execute this package.
    • What the SQL you tune uses: sequences of other schemas need SELECT ANY SEQUENCE, functions of other schemas need EXECUTE ANY PROCEDURE. Neither is part of SELECT ANY TABLE (ORA-41900 without them).
    • When a privilege is missing: the base script is a single PL/SQL block, so if any view it reads is not granted, the whole block fails to compile and nothing runs.
    • DBMS_XPLAN, DBMS_SQLTUNE, DBMS_OUTPUT and the other packages are executable by PUBLIC by default.
    PartReads
    StatisticsV$MYSTAT · V$STATNAME · GV$PX_SESSTAT · V$PARAMETER · V$DATAFILE · V$LOGFILE · V$ASM_DISKGROUP · V$CELL · V$SESS_TIME_MODEL (line 34 — without it only that line is left out)
    WaitsV$SESSION · V$SESSION_EVENT
    V$SQL · DBMS_XPLAN · QB RegistryV$SQL · V$SQL_PLAN · V$SQL_PLAN_STATISTICS_ALL
    Optimizer EnvV$SQL_OPTIMIZER_ENV
    ASHGV$ACTIVE_SESSION_HISTORY (Diagnostics Pack)
    SQL MonitorGV$SQL_MONITOR · DBMS_SQLTUNE.REPORT_SQL_MONITOR (Tuning Pack)
    SQLID → Tab · Bind VariablesV$SQL · V$SQL_BIND_CAPTURE (GV$ on RAC) · bind values from V$SQL_MONITOR (Tuning Pack) · DBA_HIST_SQLTEXT · DBA_HIST_SQLBIND (Diagnostics Pack)
    AWR in SQLID CompareDBA_HIST_SQLSTAT · DBA_HIST_SQLTEXT · DBA_HIST_ACTIVE_SESS_HISTORY (Diagnostics Pack)
    SQLID HistoryDBA_HIST_SNAPSHOT · DBA_HIST_SQLSTAT · DBA_HIST_SQLTEXT · DBA_HIST_SQLBIND · DBA_HIST_SQL_PLAN · DBA_HIST_ACTIVE_SESS_HISTORY · DBA_USERS · execute on DBMS_WORKLOAD_REPOSITORY (Diagnostics Pack) · DBA_HIST_REPORTS · DBA_HIST_REPORTS_DETAILS (Tuning Pack) · V$SQL · V$SQL_OPTIMIZER_ENV
    ObjectsV$SQL_PLAN and the ALL_* views — only objects visible to the account
    Tuning AdvisorADVISOR system privilege · GV$SQLAREA_PLAN_HASH (DBMS_SQLTUNE reads it with the caller's privileges) (Tuning Pack)
  • Windows: x64, WebView2 runtime.

13.3 Feature limits by pack licence

The two boxes in Connections decide what OraLab reads.

BoxNot read while it is off
Diagnostics Pack licensedThe ASH part of a tab run · AWR and ASH waits in SQLID Compare · AWR bind values in SQLID → Tab and Bind Variables · SQLID History (the button is disabled)
Tuning Pack licensedThe SQL Monitor report of a tab run · SQL Monitor bind values in SQLID → Tab and Bind Variables · the SQL Profile section of Plan Fix (not shown) · the Tuning Advisor sub-tab (dimmed) · the SQL Monitor tab of SQLID History

Even with a box ticked, nothing is read when the server's control_management_pack_access excludes that pack; the reason is printed instead. A tab that holds the whole base script (4.4) is your own text and does not follow the boxes — there, set v_ORALAB_ASH_ON and v_ORALAB_SQL_MONITOR to 'N' in the script yourself (the server-parameter check still works in that tab).

14. Good to know (measurements)

  • The figures are for a fetch size of 100 rows. The test SQL runs in a PL/SQL cursor, which fetches 100 rows at a time. Statistics tied to the number of fetches — consistent gets (Buffers), SQL*Net round trips and the like — therefore differ from a run in SQL*Plus (default arraysize 15) or with your application's fetch size. Keep that in mind when comparing with figures from another tool. The plan is not affected.
  • A first run includes a hard parse. When comparing, use results from a second run of each so that the conditions match (physical reads differ on a first run too).
